'''East Flatbush''' is a residential [[neighborhood]] in the [[New York City]] [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]]. East Flatbush is bounded by [[Crown Heights, Brooklyn|Crown Heights]] and Empire Boulevard to the north; [[Brownsville, Brooklyn|Brownsville]] and East 98th Street to the east; [[Flatlands, Brooklyn|Flatlands]], [[Canarsie, Brooklyn|Canarsie]] and the [[Long Island Rail Road]]'s [[Bay Ridge Branch]] to the south; and the neighborhood of [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Flatbush]] and New York Avenue to the west. East Flatbush is a predominantly black neighborhood of [[African Americans|African American]] and [[Afro-Caribbean]] persons and has a population of 135,619 as of the [[2010 United States census]].

East Flatbush is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 17|Brooklyn Community District 17]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]] is 11203.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 67th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 67th Precinct"/> Politically it is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 40th, 41st, and 45th Districts.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf "Current City Council Districts for Kings County"], [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==Geography==
As with many [[List of Brooklyn neighborhoods|neighborhoods in Brooklyn]], the borders of East Flatbush are subjective/porous, but its northern border is roughly at Empire Boulevard and [[East New York Avenue]] east of East 91st Street, its southern border is in the vicinity of the [[Long Island Rail Road]] [[Bay Ridge Branch]], its eastern border is roughly at East 98th Street and its western border is roughly at New York/Brooklyn Avenues.

East Flatbush is split up into three subsections. From west to east they are Erasmus, Farragut, and Remsen Village/Rugby.<ref name=NTAs/><ref name=NG>[https://brooklynreporter.com/nabetags/east-flatbush/ How East Flatbush Got Its Name]. By Norm Goldstein, Brooklyn Reporter.com. Accessed 11 December 2024.</ref>

===Farragut===
{{distinguish|text=[[Farragut Houses]], occasionally referred to as "Farragut" as well}}

The central section of East Flatbush is called Farragut.<ref name="NYDaily-EFlatbush-Feb2003">{{cite news|last=Perez|first=Luis|title=Working-Class Gem in Heart of City – East Flatbush's star is on the rise again|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/boroughs/working-class-gem-heart-city-east-flatbush-star-rise-article-1.662210|access-date=19 December 2016|work=[[New York Daily News]]|date=February 16, 2003}}</ref> Farragut is roughly bounded by Cortelyou Road and [[Holy Cross Cemetery, Brooklyn|Holy Cross Cemetery]] to the north, [[Kings Highway (Brooklyn)|Kings Highway]] to the east, Brooklyn Avenue on the west, and the LIRR [[Bay Ridge Branch]] to the south.<ref name=EncNYC>{{cite enc-nyc2|page=391}}</ref> Farragut was originally part of the colonial Town of Flatbush,<ref name="NYDaily-EFlatbush-Feb2003"/><ref name="EncNYC"/><ref name="NYCPks-PaerdegatPk">{{cite web|title=Paerdegat Park: History|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/paerdegat-park/history|publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]|access-date=19 December 2016}}</ref> and was named for [[American Civil War]] Admiral [[David Farragut]].<ref name=EncNYC/><ref name="NYCPks-PaerdegatPk"/> The area was largely populated by [[Jewish Americans|Jews]] and [[Italian Americans|Italians]] before 1950. By the 1990s, [[African American]]s became a majority, along with many immigrants from the [[West Indies]].<ref name=EncNYC/>

Farragut is adjacent to Paerdegat Woods, a formerly wooded area near [[Paerdegat Basin]] where real-estate developer [[Fred Trump]] constructed housing in the 1940s.<ref name="NYCPks-PaerdegatPk"/><ref name="NYTimes-Paerdegat-Trump-1940">{{cite news|title=Brooklyn 'Forest' Is Site For Homes: Paerdegat Woods in Flatbush Section Giving Way to Trump's Project|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1940/05/19/94830052.html|access-date=July 12, 2026|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=May 19, 1940|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Farragut also contains Flatbush Gardens (formerly named Vanderveer Estates),<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vitullo-Martin|first=Julia|date=March 15, 2007|title=A Once-Troubled Housing Complex Seeks Change|url=https://www.nysun.com/real-estate/once-troubled-housing-complex-seeks-change/50520/|access-date=2021-09-06|website=The New York Sun}}</ref> a 59-building complex erected in 1949.<ref name="NYDaily-EFlatbush-Feb2003"/><ref name="EncNYC"/><ref name="NYCPks-PaerdegatPk"/><ref>{{cite news|last=Goodman|first=George W.|title=Brooklyn Rehabilitation Draws Fire|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/09/04/realestate/brooklyn-rehabilitation-draws-fire.html|access-date=19 December 2016|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=September 4, 1983}}</ref> Vanderveer Estates was built on the site of the old Flatbush Water Works.<ref name="Newman Brick 2004">{{cite web | last1=Newman | first1=Andy | last2=Brick | first2=Michael | title=A Long-Troubled Complex Hopes to Flourish Again | website=The New York Times | date=January 13, 2004 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/01/13/nyregion/a-long-troubled-complex-hopes-to-flourish-again.html | access-date=March 9, 2019|name-list-style=and}}</ref> The complex is one of the largest privately held working-class housing complexes in New York City, and owned in part by [[David Bistricer]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Buckley|first=Cara|date=2010-12-11|title=Violations and Lockout Mire Brooklyn Complex|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/11/nyregion/11flatbush.html|access-date=2021-09-06|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Notable people who once lived in Vanderveer Estates include [[Barbra Streisand]]<ref name="Newman Brick 2004"/> and [[Michael K. Williams]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Remnick|first=Noah|date=2017-06-30|title=Michael K. Williams Is More Than Omar From 'The Wire'|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/30/nyregion/michael-k-williams-is-more-than-omar-from-the-wire.html|access-date=2021-09-06|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

===Remsen Village===
Remsen Village has been described as a "subsection of the larger East Flatbush neighborhood,"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://brooklynmls.com/remsen-village |title=Remsen Village |access-date=March 9, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190413235042/https://www.brooklynmls.com/remsen-village/ |archive-date=April 13, 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref> with an estimated 60,000 residents.<ref name=Pop60>{{Cite web|url=http://www.city-data.com/neighborhood/Remsen-Village-Brooklyn-NY.html|title=Remsen Village neighborhood in Brooklyn, New York (NY), 11236, 11203, 11212, 11213 subdivision profile - real estate, apartments, condos, homes, community, population, jobs, income, streets|website=city-data.com}}</ref> but is also sometimes considered its own neighborhood<ref name="NYTimes-GirlKilled-2001">{{cite news |title=Metro Briefing, Brooklyn - Girl Shot and Killed |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/10/01/nyregion/metro-briefing-new-york-brooklyn-girl-shot-and-killed.html |last1=Wakin |first1=Daniel J. |last2=Ramirez |newspaper=The New York Times |date=October 1, 2001|name-list-style=and|first2=Anthony}}</ref> and also as "Rugby-Remsen Village".<ref>{{cite web |website=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2016/04/20/us/politics/best-nyc-neighborhoods-for-each-presidential-candidate.html |title=The New York City Neighborhoods That Love Each Candidate |last1=Watkins |last2=Parlapiano |date=April 20, 2016|first=Derek|first2=Alicia|name-list-style=and}}</ref> The origin of using the name ''Remsen Village'' seems to be in the mid-1990s.<ref>{{cite news |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/04/30/realestate/l-neighborhoods-the-sacred-sites-925195.html |title=Neighborhoods: The 'Sacred Sites' |date=April 30, 1995}}</ref> Remsen Village's population<ref name=Pop60/> is over one third of that of [[Brooklyn Community Board 17]], which consists entirely of East Flatbush and its subsections.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/cau/html/cb/cb_brooklyn.shtml |title=Brooklyn Community Boards |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071221003420/http://www.nyc.gov/html/cau/html/cb/cb_brooklyn.shtml |archive-date=December 21, 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The name "Rugby" was described in 2016 by ''The New York Times'' as "the old name for the area." It persists as the name of a road in East Flatbush, as well as a library branch in eastern East Flatbush.<ref>{{cite web |website=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/11/06/travel/brooklyn-budget-frugal-travel.html |title=Want the 'Real' Brooklyn? Go Cheap |last=Peterson |date=November 11, 2016|first=Lucas}}</ref> The name "Rugby" was chosen by developers in the 1890s.<ref name=NG/>

==Demographics==
East Flatbush is divided into three neighborhood tabulation areas (Erasmus, Farragut, and Remsen Village), which collectively comprise the population of the area.<ref name=NTAs>[https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/ntas.pdf New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref> Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the combined population of East Flatbush's neighborhood tabulation areas was 135,619, a change of −9,740 (−7.2%) from the 145,359 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{cvt|1871.5|acre}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|72.5|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name=PLP5>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

The [[Race and ethnicity in the United States census|racial makeup]] of the neighborhood was 1.3% (1,816) White, 88.7% (120,231) African American, 0.3% (366) Native American, 1.1% (1,480) Asian, 0% (45) Pacific Islander, 0.4% (523) from other races, and 1.6% (2,140) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. census)|Latino]] of any race were 6.6% (9,018) of the population.<ref name=PLP3A>[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

The entirety of Community Board 17 had 154,575 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 82.6 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-bk17.pdf|title=East Flatbush (Including East Flatbush, Eramus, Farragut, Northeast Flatbush, Remsen Village and Rugby)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is higher than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017|archive-date=September 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004755/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}}<ref>{{cite web | title=New Yorkers are living longer, happier and healthier lives | website=New York Post | last=Short | first=Aaron | date=June 4, 2017 | url=https://nypost.com/2017/06/04/new-yorkers-are-living-longer-happier-and-healthier-lives/ | access-date=March 1, 2019}}</ref> Most inhabitants are middle-aged adults and youth: 21% are between the ages of 0 and 17, 28% between 25 and 44, and 28% between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 9% and 15%, respectively.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|2}}

As of 2016, the median [[household income]] in Community District 17 was $49,349.<ref>{{cite web|title=Census profile:NYC-Brooklyn Community District 17--East Flatbush, Farragut & Rugby PUMA, NY|website=Census Reporter|date=July 22, 2018|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604010-nyc-brooklyn-community-district-17-east-flatbush-farragut-rugby-puma-ny/|access-date=July 22, 2018|archive-date=August 25, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825003838/https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604010-nyc-brooklyn-community-district-17-east-flatbush-farragut-rugby-puma-ny/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 19% of East Flatbush residents lived in poverty, compared to 21% in all of Brooklyn and 20% in all of New York City. One in eleven residents (9%) were unemployed, compared to 9% in the rest of both Brooklyn and New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 54% in East Flatbush, higher than the citywide and boroughwide rates of 52% and 51%, respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, East Flatbush is considered to be high-income and not [[gentrification|gentrifying]], relative to the rest of the city.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|7}}

===Ethnic groups and subsections===
East Flatbush generally is very similar in nature to neighboring [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Flatbush]], as both are predominantly West Indian and working class; however, Flatbush has a higher percentage of White and Asian residents than East Flatbush. The area was populated after [[World War II]] predominantly by immigrant [[Jews]] and [[Italians]], then in the 1960s by [[African Americans]], but most recently has seen many West Indian immigrants such as [[Guyana|Guyanese]], [[Haiti]]ans, [[Jamaica]]ns, [[St. Lucia|Saint Lucians]], [[Trinidad and Tobago|Trinidadians]], [[Grenada|Grenadians]], [[Saint Vincent and the Grenadines|Vincentians]], [[Barbados|Bajans]], [[Panama]]nians and [[Dominican Republic|Dominicans]] groups coming to the area. Within its confines is the [[Holy Cross Cemetery, Brooklyn]], which is located at 3620 Tilden Avenue. While some residents are affluent, East Flatbush is mostly populated by working and middle-class Brooklynites. Similar to other eastern Brooklyn neighborhoods, Blacks predominate East Flatbush. The area is 91.4% Black or African-American<ref>{{cite web |url=http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/SAFFFacts?_event=ChangeGeoContext&geo_id=86000US11203&_geoContext=01000US%7C04000US36%7C05000US36047&_street=&_county=&_cityTown=&_state=04000US36&_zip=11203&_lang=en&_sse=on&ActiveGeoDiv=geoSelect&_useEV=&pctxt=fph&pgsl=010&_submenuId=factsheet_1&ds_name=DEC_2000_SAFF&_ci_nbr=null&qr_name=null&reg=null:null&_keyword=&_industry= |title=American FactFinder - Community Facts |website=factfinder.census.gov |access-date=27 January 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200212053125/http://factfinder.census.gov/servlet/SAFFFacts?_event=ChangeGeoContext&geo_id=86000US11203&_geoContext=01000US%7C04000US36%7C05000US36047&_street=&_county=&_cityTown=&_state=04000US36&_zip=11203&_lang=en&_sse=on&ActiveGeoDiv=geoSelect&_useEV=&pctxt=fph&pgsl=010&_submenuId=factsheet_1&ds_name=DEC_2000_SAFF&_ci_nbr=null&qr_name=null&reg=null:null&_keyword=&_industry= |archive-date=12 February 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and 51% foreign born,<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2003nhp-brooklyng.pdf "Community Health Profiles: The Health of Flatbush, Brooklyn"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121107101227/http://www.nyc.gov/html/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2003nhp-brooklyng.pdf |date=November 7, 2012 }}, nyc.gov</ref> the majority of whom are from the Caribbean. Considering this data, East Flatbush has been noted as being the single largest West Indian neighborhood in all of New York City and America as a whole.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2c76ubuRGRwC&q=flatbush+%22most+west+indian%22&pg=PA49|title=The West Indian Americans|isbn=9780313310096|last=Henke|first=Holger|year=2001|publisher=Bloomsbury Academic }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://on.aol.com/video/-mike-and-molly--star-reno-wilson-on-his-caribbean-heritage-517830688|title='Mike and Molly' Star Reno Wilson On His Caribbean Heritage|work=aol.on}}</ref>

According to the 2020 census data from [[New York City Department of City Planning]], East Flatbush has been given three different names for three different sections, which are East Flatbush Erasmus to the west, East Flatbush Farragut to the east, and East Flatbush Rugby to the north. The Erasmus portion had between 30,000 and 39,999 Black residents and between 5,000 and 9,999 Hispanic residents, meanwhile each the White and Asian populations were fewer than 5,000 residents. The Rugby portion had 30,000 to 39,999 Black residents while each the Hispanic, White, and Asian populations were all fewer than 5,000 residents. The Farragut portion had 20,000 to 29,999 Black residents while each the Hispanic, White, and Asian population were also all fewer than 5,000 residents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2020/dcp_2020-census-briefing-booklet-1.pdf|title=Key Population & Housing Characteristics; 2020 Census Results for New York City|publisher=[[New York City Department of City Planning]]|date=August 2021|access-date=November 7, 2021|pages=21, 25, 29, 33}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Map: Race and ethnicity across the US | website=CNN | date=August 14, 2021 | url=https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2021/us/census-race-ethnicity-map/ | access-date=November 7, 2021}}</ref>

=== Little Caribbean and Little Haiti ===
{{See also|Little Caribbean, Brooklyn|Little Haiti, Brooklyn}}
Since the 1960s and especially through the 1970s, Caribbean immigrants have largely settled into East Flatbush, as well as in other surrounding areas such as [[Flatbush, Brooklyn|Flatbush]] and [[Crown Heights, Brooklyn|Crown Heights]]. Since 2017, the areas surrounding Nostrand and Church Avenues have been given the nickname [[Little Caribbean, Brooklyn|Little Caribbean]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.littlecaribbean.nyc/|title=Little Caribbean NYC|website=Little Caribbean NYC}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170926/flatbush/flatbush-little-caribbean-neighborhood-designation|title=Flatbush to Become City's First 'Little Caribbean' Neighborhood This Week|website=DNAinfo New York|access-date=July 19, 2021|archive-date=July 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718180736/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170926/flatbush/flatbush-little-caribbean-neighborhood-designation/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.garrettleight.com/blogs/stories/neighborhood-guide-brooklyn-s-little-caribbean|title=Neighborhood Guide: Brooklyn's Little Caribbean|website=Garrett Leight|date=April 29, 2021 }}</ref> In addition to Little Caribbean, the south tip of the neighborhood has been given the name [[Little Haiti, Brooklyn|Little Haiti]] due to the high concentration of Haitians.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.littlehaitibk.org/|title=Little Haiti Bk | Home|website=littlehaitibk.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bklyner.com/little-caribbean-v-little-haiti-not-so-simple-to-brand-flatbush/|title=Little Caribbean v Little Haiti - Not So Simple to Designate a Cultural Area in Flatbush|date=September 28, 2017}}</ref> Additionally, the [[Newkirk Avenue–Little Haiti station]] of the [[New York City Subway]]'s {{NYCS trains|Nostrand}} was formally renamed from Newkirk Avenue in 2021.<ref>{{cite web | title=MTA renames Newkirk Avenue 2/5 station to Newkirk Avenue-Little Haiti | website=Brooklyn Eagle | date=November 18, 2021 | url=https://brooklyneagle.com/articles/2021/11/18/mta-renames-newkirk-avenue-2-5-station-to-newkirk-avenue-little-haiti/ | access-date=December 9, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Ross | first=Michelle | title=Haitian community celebrates heritage with Brooklyn subway renaming | website=PIX11 | date=November 19, 2021 | url=https://pix11.com/news/local-news/haitian-community-celebrates-heritage-with-brooklyn-subway-renaming/ | access-date=December 9, 2021}}</ref>

== Police and crime ==
The [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]]'s 67th Precinct (known internally by NYPD officers as Fort Jah<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-defends-challenge-coins-dubbing-east-flatbush-precinct-fort-jah|title=NYPD Defends Challenge Coins Dubbing East Flatbush Fort Jah|date=August 30, 2020|access-date=December 3, 2020}}</ref>) is located at 2820 Snyder Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 67th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/67th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 67th Precinct|website=nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 67th Precinct ranked 40th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref name=":18">{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/east-flatbush|title=East Flatbush – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306111529/https://www.dnainfo.com/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/east-flatbush/|archive-date=March 6, 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 80 per 100,000 people, East Flatbush's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is greater than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 597 per 100,000 people is higher than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|8}} The Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 79.9% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported 6 murders, 43 rapes, 246 robberies, 601 felony assaults, 225 burglaries, 586 grand larcenies, and 98 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-067pct.pdf|title=67th Precinct CompStat Report|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

A drug epidemic ravaged East Flatbush during the late 1970s, 1980s and early 1990s, mostly in Vanderveer Estates. The intersection of Foster Avenue and Nostrand Avenues was nicknamed "the Front Page" because of media attention to drug murders there. The intersection of Foster between New York Avenue and Brooklyn Avenue area to the south was called "the Back Page" because its many murders went unnoticed.<ref>Vitullo-Martin, Julia. [http://www.nysun.com/real-estate/once-troubled-housing-complex-seeks-change/50520/ "A Once-Troubled Housing Complex Seeks Change: Flatbush Gardens"], ''[[The New York Sun]]'', March 15, 2007. Accessed May 2, 2016. "A criminologist and professor of anthropology at John Jay College who produced a report on crime for the Brooklyn district attorney in 2003, Ric Curtis, said Vanderveer residents nicknamed the intersection of Foster and Nostrand avenues 'the Front Page' because the drug murders there often ended up on the front pages of local papers."</ref> The area around the Nostrand playground had various gangs: [[Crips]], [[Gangster Disciples]], [[Jamaicans]] ([[Shower Posse]]), [[Trinidadians]] and [[Grenadians]] particularly notorious for turf wars, shootouts, and pitbull fights. Crime is still somewhat of a problem in the neighborhood today as well.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

== Health ==
[[File:Univ Hosp Bklyn Lenox jeh.JPG|thumb|SUNY Downstate Medical Center]]
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers are more common in East Flatbush than in other places citywide. In East Flatbush, there were 126 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 20.6 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|11}} East Flatbush has a high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]], or who receive healthcare through [[Medicaid]].<ref name=":14">[http://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/dsrip/pps_applications/docs/maimonides_medical_center/3.8_maimonides_cna.pdf New York City Health Provider Partnership Brooklyn Community Needs Assessment: Final Report], [[New York Academy of Medicine]] (October 3, 2014).</ref> In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 15%, which is higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in East Flatbush is {{convert|0.0078|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, lower than the citywide and boroughwide averages.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|9}} Eight percent of East Flatbush residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is lower the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|13}} In East Flatbush, 34% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 15% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 36% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28%, respectively.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|16}} In addition, 22% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|12}}

Eighty percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is lower than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 83% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", higher than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in East Flatbush, there are 21 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|10}}

East Flatbush is home to three major hospitals, [[Kings County Hospital]], [[SUNY Downstate Medical Center]], and [[Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center]].<ref name=":14"/>

==Transportation==
East Flatbush does not have as much access to the [[New York City Subway]] as Flatbush. However, the [[IRT Nostrand Avenue Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Nostrand}}) has some stops located near the western border of East Flatbush, particularly [[Newkirk Avenue–Little Haiti station|Newkirk Avenue–Little Haiti]], [[Beverly Road (IRT Nostrand Avenue Line)|Beverly Road]], and [[Church Avenue (IRT Nostrand Avenue Line)|Church Avenue]].<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> Additionally, along the neighborhood's eastern border with Brownsville, the [[IRT New Lots Line]] ({{NYCS trains|New Lots day}}) has a [[Sutter Avenue–Rutland Road station|station]] at the intersection of Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road, and East 98th Street.

[[MTA Regional Bus Operations]]' {{NYC bus link|B44|B44 SBS|B46|B46 SBS|prose=y}} routes run north–south through East Flatbush, while the {{NYC bus link|B6|B8|B35|prose=y}} run east–west. The [[B12 (New York City bus)|B12]] bus takes a serpentine route at the north end of the neighborhood as well as the [[B43 (New York City bus)|B43]], and the {{NYC bus link|B7}} runs on [[Kings Highway (Brooklyn)|Kings Highway]] at the southeast edge of East Flatbush.<ref>{{cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref> The B6 runs via Bay Pkwy, Avenue J, and Flatlands Av and although passing through several neighborhoods, makes a few stops in East Flatbush. The {{NYC bus link|B103|BM2|prose=y}} also makes a few stops in the area on Avenue H, by the border with [[Flatlands, Brooklyn|Flatlands]].

==Education==
East Flatbush generally has a lower ratio of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 30% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 15% have less than a high school education and 55% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 40% of Brooklynites and 38% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}} The percentage of East Flatbush students excelling in math has been increasing, with math achievement rising from 32 percent in 2000 to 51 percent in 2011, though reading achievement within the same time period stayed steady at 42%.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/BK_17_11.pdf|title=East Flatbush – BK 17|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

East Flatbush's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is slightly higher than the rest of New York City. In East Flatbush, 23% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], compared to the citywide average of 20% of students.<ref name=":21"/>{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 78% of high school students in East Flatbush graduate on time, higher than the citywide average of 75% of students.<ref name="CHP2018"/>{{Rp|6}}

===Libraries===
The [[Brooklyn Public Library]] (BPL) has two branches in East Flatbush. The Rugby branch is located at 1000 [[Utica Avenue]] and opened in 1957.<ref>{{cite web | title=Rugby Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 22, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/rugby | access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> It was closed for renovations in 2017<ref name="Blau Sandoval 2019 g460">{{cite web | last1=Blau | first1=Reuven | last2=Sandoval | first2=Gabriel | title=Patrons at the Rugby branch are relegated to a trailer and frustrations rise over the city's longest ongoing library renovation project. | website=The City | date=August 19, 2019 | url=https://www.thecity.nyc/2019/08/19/neverending-story-brooklyn-library-revamp-drags-14-years/ | access-date=December 16, 2023}}</ref> and reopened in 2021.<ref name="Brachfeld 2021 z046">{{cite web | last=Brachfeld | first=Ben | title=Closed Since 2017, Rugby Library in East Flatbush Reopens After Long-Awaited Renovation | website=Brownstoner | date=July 14, 2021 | url=https://www.brownstoner.com/brooklyn-life/east-flatbush-brooklyn-public-library-rugby-branch-1000-utica-avenue-reopens-after-renovation/ | access-date=December 16, 2023}}</ref>

The East Flatbush Library is located at 9612 Church Avenue, between East 96th Street and [[Rockaway Parkway]], and was opened in 1945. In September 2018, this library was also closed for renovations;<ref>{{cite web | title=East Flatbush Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 19, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/east-flatbush | access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref> it reopened in June 2023.<ref name="Schillaci 2023 q794">{{cite web | last=Schillaci | first=Trevor | title=LEVENBETTS design pleated aluminum facade for East Flatbush Library | website=The Architect’s Newspaper | date=November 3, 2023 | url=https://www.archpaper.com/2023/11/levenbetts-pleated-aluminum-facade-east-flatbush-library/ | access-date=December 16, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Ginsburg 2023 i247">{{cite web | last=Ginsburg | first=Aaron | title=East Flatbush's new library is light-filled and inviting | website=6sqft | date=June 9, 2023 | url=https://www.6sqft.com/east-flatbush-library-reopens-after-renovation/ | access-date=December 16, 2023}}</ref>
